texas-football.summary: Texas opened with a 59-7 win, but left guard is still a rotation and Derrek Cooper will miss Ohio State. The Buckeyes visit Saturday at 6:30 p.m. CT on ABC; watch the protection inside and whether the defense can keep creating takeaways.

items.headline: Cooper will miss Ohio State; the third-back snaps open up
items.tldr: Sarkisian says Derrek Cooper remains in a walking boot, with no return date announced. Hollywood Smothers and Raleek Brown still lead the backfield; watch who spells them after Michael Terry III and James Simon each got three carries in the opener.

items.headline: Sikorski and Seymore will keep sharing left guard
items.tldr: Dylan Sikorski started and played 33 snaps against Texas State; Laurence Seymore played 36, and Sarkisian expects the rotation to continue. With Cole Hutson still ineligible, watch whether that pairing can protect the pocket and open running lanes against Ohio State.

items.headline: Biles forced a fumble and intercepted a screen in his Texas debut
items.tldr: Rasheem Biles punched the ball loose for Graceson Littleton's 59-yard touchdown return, then read a tunnel screen for an interception. Against Ohio State, watch his recognition underneath as well as his pass rush: both takeaways came from plays beyond blitzing the quarterback.

items.headline: Manning opens with four touchdown passes and eight different receivers
items.tldr: Arch Manning threw for 305 yards in the 59-7 win, with Ryan Wingo catching seven passes for 121 yards and Cam Coleman scoring twice. That gives the passing game something to build on against Ohio State, which visits September 12 at 6:30 p.m. CT on ABC.

items.headline: DKR's new map puts gates, water stations and first aid on your phone
items.tldr: The interactive stadium map is available in the Texas Longhorns app and on the web, with seats, concessions, restrooms and fan activities marked. Open it before arriving Saturday to find what you need; step-by-step wayfinding is still listed as coming soon.

lead.headline: Protect the pocket. Win up front.
lead.body: Ohio State is next after a 59-7 opener. Watch the left-guard rotation, protection inside, and whether the defense can keep taking the ball away.

matchup.question: How does Texas take control early?
matchup.answer: Watch first and second down. If Texas stays ahead of the sticks and wins up front, the whole offense opens up.

notes.title: Early downs: stay on schedule
notes.body: Early downs are the cleanest tell for this offense. When runs and quick throws keep Texas ahead of the sticks, the whole playbook opens up. Too many third-and-longs mean trouble.

notes.title: Interior line: find the best five
notes.body: Left guard remains a rotation between Dylan Sikorski and Laurence Seymore after the opener, as Sarkisian confirmed Monday. Watch short yardage and protection against interior pressure to see who earns more snaps against Ohio State.

notes.title: Clean start: checks, snaps, ball security
notes.body: The quarterback's first job is simple: get the call right, snap it on time, and protect the ball. Field position matters more than one highlight throw on Saturday.

notes.title: Pressure with four
notes.body: If the front can pressure with four, Texas can keep more help in coverage. Watch early downs and how often the defense needs a fifth rusher to move the quarterback.

notes.title: Ohio State: the first big test
notes.body: Ohio State is the first big test up front. Texas has to stay on schedule and protect without helping on every snap.

notes.title: Texas State: opener watch list
notes.body: Texas State will test tackling in space and the defense's response to tempo. Watch early downs, who gets real snaps, and whether Texas wins up front.

utah-state-football.summary: Utah State heads to Washington after a 29-17 loss to Idaho State. Hillstead's forearm and Brosterhous's planned role make quarterback usage worth watching, but four interceptions and repeated penalties leave the whole offense with work to do before Saturday's 1:30 p.m. MT kickoff.

items.headline: Hillstead's forearm affected his throws; Brosterhous has a weekly role
items.tldr: Mendenhall said Monday that McCae Hillstead's forearm trouble worsened during the opener and affected his velocity and accuracy. He also said Grady Brosterhous will play in every game under a plan that predates the loss, so a change at quarterback Saturday would not by itself signal a new starter.

items.headline: Eleven penalties leave the offense work to do before its first road game
items.tldr: Utah State drew 11 flags for 83 yards despite practicing with crowd noise and late-game situations during camp. Mendenhall says that preparation needs more work; watch whether the offense can get lined up and snap cleanly in Seattle before judging its ability to sustain drives.

items.headline: Four interceptions wipe out Utah State's yardage advantage
items.tldr: The Aggies outgained Idaho State 407-241 but lost 29-17, with the Bengals scoring 10 points after turnovers. Ball security is the first test at Washington: moving the ball means little if the next possession gives the opponent a short field.

items.headline: Washington kicks off at 1:30 p.m. Mountain on Big Ten Network
items.tldr: Saturday's road game is at Husky Stadium in Seattle, where the local kickoff time is 12:30 p.m. Pacific. Utah State's game guide puts the broadcast, radio stream, live stats and game notes in one place, so check your Big Ten Network access before kickoff.

items.headline: Eli Wood leads Utah State's receivers with six catches
items.tldr: Wood caught six passes for 90 yards and a touchdown, while Demick Starling added three catches and the other receiving score. Those are two names to follow as Utah State tries to make its passing game more consistent.

lead.headline: Protect the ball. Make them drive.
lead.body: Four interceptions helped turn the opener into a 29-17 loss. Washington is next: watch the quarterback rotation, clean snaps, and tackling in space.

matchup.question: How does Utah State stay in the game at Washington?
matchup.answer: Protect the ball and keep Demond Williams Jr. contained. When he extends a play, the secondary has to stay with its receivers.

utah-state-football.notesDisclaimer: Section One notes are independent. Each note is dated and should be read with linked team sources.

notes.title: Run game: stay ahead of the chains
notes.body: The run game sets up everything else for this offense. When Utah State stays ahead of the chains on early downs, tempo and play-action both become real options instead of hopes. Third-and-long is where a drive in Logan goes to die.

notes.title: Quarterback play: protect the ball, protect the field
notes.body: The quarterback's first job here is field position, not highlights. Get the call in on time, take the checkdown, and make the other team drive the length of the field. One free turnover swings a game Utah State would otherwise play even.

notes.title: Explosive plays: the number that decides these games
notes.body: Explosive plays are the cleanest tell for this defense. Utah State can live with long, slow drives against it; what it cannot live with is giving up chunk plays behind coverage. Watch how often a safety ends up as the last line.

notes.title: Special teams: the cheapest points on the field
notes.body: Special teams is the cheapest place on the field to win yards. A net punt edge and clean kick coverage are worth more to Utah State than any single play call. Field position is how a team without a talent edge is still in a game in the fourth quarter.

notes.title: Pac-12 move: a harder Saturday most weeks
notes.body: The Pac-12 move means a harder Saturday most weeks than the old slate held. The line of scrimmage is where that shows up first, and it shows up late in games before it shows up early. Depth up front matters more in November than it does in September.

notes.title: Washington: contain the quarterback
notes.body: Washington visits are a test of ball security and discipline. Mendenhall identified Demond Williams Jr. as a quarterback who needs multiple defenders to contain him; Brevin Hamblin emphasized staying on top of routes when Williams extends plays. Watch rush lanes and whether the secondary stays with its receivers in Seattle.
